newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Funds want Deutsche Telekom but expect no bargain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Funds want Deutsche Telekom but expect no bargain.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom, Europe's biggest privatisation yet, is seen as a "must-have" stock by British institutions but none expect to land a bargain and many have longer term reservations about the company. The 500 million share offer, or 20 percent of the company, is the sector's largest since British Telecom in 1984.
"It's a groundbreaking issue, the first in Continental Europe since the old-style British privatisations of the 1980s," said Tony Parker, European fund manager at Kleinwort Benson.
He said the case for buying Deutsche Telekom (DT) by German institutional and retail investors was "compelling" because of tax benefits. "But for an outsider there is no such advantage."

"The only criteria DT is cheap on is yield," noted a US fund manager in London. "For all others it is at the top end of the range. We'll take some but it's not a bargain. It is priced pretty fully for a company with lots of questions over it."
Some 600 million sterling ($985.4 million), or up to 12 percent of the offer is being targeted at UK institutional investors.
While the two-year outlook for DT is relatively rosy, fund managers have two major concerns about the company -- its huge debt and the spectre of deregulation after 1998.
HOW WILL IT FARE IN PRIVATE HANDS?

"There's also a lot of value being based on their ability to make a smooth transition from a bureaucratic public utility to a dynamic international entrepreneurial business," said Tony Zucker, head of European equities at Friends Provident.
The key question for European funds is why they should buy DT over all other telecoms stock available, and at what price.

Other operators in the crowded sector are British Telecom, now set to challenge after its merger with MCI Communications, Ireland's Telecomm Eirann, Belgian carrier Belgacom, Spain's Telefonica and its Unisource alliance, STET of Italy, Tele Danmark and France Telecom.

Portugal Telecom, with 49.2 percent floated in 1995 and 1996, has grown by nearly 20 percent in H1 1996 alone, according to ABN-Amro Hoare Govett, largely on its strategic links with potential high-growth markets like Brazil.
DT scores well in this area, with joint ventures across Asia and a 67 percent stake with Ameritech in Hungary's Matav which plans a $500 million IPO itself in the next 18 months.
Kleinwort's Parker said funds would judge each issue on its own merits. "Our job is to make money for our investors. If you think that will happen you sell other holdings and buy in."
So will funds dump other Euro-telecoms stock to buy DT?
"If they are going to sell to accomodate DT they will have done it already," said a European privatisation manager who declined to be named.
"We have seen other stocks like (Dutch telecoms) KPM take the odd dip as holdings are trimmed but if the sector is generally favoured DT is more likely to drag the others up."
HARD TO ASSESS VALUE OF DT STOCK
But many will be angling for as big a slice as possible. The stock will form a significant part of the DAX index, which will draw index-tracking and general European equity funds.

A Scottish fund manager said DT was also clearly a global play like BT, rather than a regional or national stock. That has been underlined by DT's recent statement that it may list in Singapore and Hong Kong as well as Frankfurt and New York.
Everyone agrees the issue will be heavily oversubscribed but fair value is difficult to call. "It is where it's priced, no-one is expecting a discount as such," lamented one.
Parker said it would be determined partly by what yield German investors required. "If they want four percent it will be 40 marks ($26.54) but if they want five it will be not much above 34."

Others said fair value would depend on expectations of future revenue. The grey market price of around 35 marks is already seen as overvalued but a big unknown is how the three million German retail investors who could hold stock will act.
"Are they going to sell up straight after, like the British did?" said Parker. "In the past they have stuck to yield investments like bonds but this has a good income flow."

Jamie Sanderson, head of European equities at Edinburgh Fund Managers said retail investors were being heavily sold the attractive dividend yield. They will probably hang on for the first dividend in 1997 and the more lucrative second one in 1998, which could precipitate a price squeeze.
"There is no question everyone is going to buy, it's when to sell which is the problem," said the privatisation fund manager.
